4a(1).fact: Rowers must step directly onto the centerline of the hull floor along the keel while keeping their center of gravity low to avoid tipping the craft.
4a(1).misconception: Stepping onto the nearest thwart or gunwale provides the most stable footing when climbing aboard a floating rowboat.
4a(1).pamphlet_summary: Before boarding, the boat should be floating clear of the bottom while the rower steps squarely onto the centerline along the keel rather than onto a gunwale or thwart. The painter must remain secured or in hand, and oars should be shipped in rowlocks and boated or trailed until the craft clears shoreline obstructions (p. 28).
4a(1).socratic_question: Why is it essential to step directly onto the centerline of the boat bottom rather than onto a seat or gunwale when boarding?

4a(2).fact: Aligning two stationary shore features in a line over the stern as range marks allows rowers to maintain a straight course without constantly turning around.
4a(2).misconception: Twisting around to look over your shoulder on every stroke is the best way to steer a rowboat in a straight line.
4a(2).pamphlet_summary: Rowers maintain a straight course across open water by aligning two stationary landmarks over the stern as range marks while pulling evenly with both oars. Stopping the craft requires holding water by squaring blades against forward motion, followed by pushing one oar while pulling the other to pivot the boat in place (p. 32).
4a(2).socratic_question: How can you use two stationary objects on shore behind you to keep your rowboat traveling in a perfectly straight line?

4a(3).fact: A turn underway is performed while maintaining forward boat speed by pulling harder with one oar or trailing the opposite blade to carve a smooth arc.
4a(3).misconception: Executing an underway turn requires bringing the rowboat to a dead stop and reversing one oar against the other.
4a(3).pamphlet_summary: Backwatering propels the rowboat stern-first by pushing the oar handles forward from the chest with squared blades buried in the water. Making a turn underway requires maintaining headway while pulling harder on one oar or trailing the opposite blade to swing the bow smoothly without coming to a stop (p. 35).
4a(3).socratic_question: How does the way you handle your oars during a turn underway differ from how you turn when pivoting in place?

4a(4).fact: Landing into the wind or current allows natural water resistance to slow the boat while preserving positive directional control at low speed.
4a(4).misconception: Approaching a dock downwind at full speed gives the craft the maximum steerage needed for a controlled landing.
4a(4).pamphlet_summary: Approaching a dock safely requires easing speed by holding water and angling into the wind or current at roughly forty-five degrees to retain rudderless steerage. Once alongside, rowers ship their oars before stepping ashore, then secure the craft with the painter or stow the hull inverted on an onshore rack (p. 38).
4a(4).socratic_question: Why does an experienced rower always prefer to approach a dock headed into the wind or current rather than with it?

4a(5).fact: Mooring requires dedicated knots like the roundturn with two half-hitches or bowline because wave surges easily capsize or untie standard square knots.
4a(5).misconception: Any standard utility knot like a square knot will hold a rowboat securely to a dock piling under wave action.
4a(5).pamphlet_summary: Mooring knots secure the boat painter to pilings, rings, or cleats while resisting wave surge and allowing a quick release when casting off. The bowline forms a fixed nonslip loop, the roundturn with two half-hitches locks securely under heavy surging, and the Wellman's knot and mooring hitch provide reliable quick-release options for temporary ties (p. 42).
4a(5).socratic_question: Which mooring knot would you select if your boat is tied to a rough wooden piling in heavy chop where you need both security and a fast castoff?
